\subsection{Transfer-learning protocol}
\label{sec:sota-protocol}

Two pretrained lightweight architectures were adapted to EuroSAT:
MobileNetV2~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2} and
EfficientNet-B0~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}.
Both were initialised with ImageNet weights, and the final linear layer of each
classifier was replaced by a
new ten-class prediction layer. Every run used the same stratified split, random
seed, augmentation, training-split normalisation statistics, batch size of 128,
30-epoch budget and Colab Tesla~T4 as Models~A and~B.
The checkpoint was chosen by lowest validation loss, before testing.

After adding the new prediction layer, there were two options: keep the
pretrained backbone \emph{frozen}, or \emph{fine-tune} it. Each network was
tested with both, to determine whether fine-tuning all parameters gives a gain.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Frozen.} In this case, only the new prediction layer was trained, with Adam at
  a learning rate of $10^{-3}$. The CNN backbone was used as a fixed feature
  extractor,
  with its batch-normalisation statistics held at their original ImageNet values.
  \item \textbf{Fine-tuned.} In this case, every weight was trained, starting from the
  ImageNet weights, with Adam using a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. Here we chose
  a smaller learning rate
 than the frozen-backbone rate to limit changes to the pretrained filters while
  the new classifier learns.
\end{itemize}

Our main runs kept the input at $64\times64$, the original resolution that the
custom models see: the only like-for-like comparison with Model~B, and the input
an edge device would be given. Because ImageNet networks are
designed for $224\times224$ input, the experiment was repeated for each network
with the $64\times64$ images upsampled to $224\times224$, for both the frozen
and fine-tuned cases. Each $224\times224$
pair differs from its original pair in input size only, so as to identify the
effect of matching the input to the resolution that the pretrained networks were
trained on.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:sota-results}

  \centering

  % box \generatedtable shows before the runs exist cannot sit in a \resizebox.
  \footnotesize
  \setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
  \generatedtable{tables/sota_comparison.tex}{\#22}
  \caption{Pretrained lightweight models on the EuroSAT test split. Precision
  and recall are macro averages over the ten classes. \emph{Trained} counts the
  parameters updated during training. Sizes are in MB, measured from the saved
  weights; the custom models in Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison} are in KB.
  The supplementary rows upsample the $64\times64$ images to $224\times224$.}
  \label{tab:sota-comparison}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:sota-comparison} shows results obtained with both the frozen and
fine-tuned configurations for each of the two networks. \emph{Parameters} and
\emph{Size} are
the same for the frozen and fine-tuned runs of the same network. Freezing only
changes which parameters are trained, so the difference is in the \emph{Trained}
column. Accuracy gaps between the two rows of a pair are therefore obtained with
training effort only, at no cost in memory or in operations per image.

We observed that for both networks that accuracy gap is large: fine-tuning
raises every metric well above the frozen case. The likely explanation is the
domain shift from ImageNet to satellite images.
ImageNet filters were learnt on close-range photographs of objects, while
EuroSAT consists of overhead satellite images at a much smaller scale.
A frozen backbone can only re-weight features learnt for the wrong kind of
image, whereas fine-tuning lets the filters adapt to field boundaries, road
textures and water.

With the backbone frozen, EfficientNet-B0 is the weaker network, despite having
almost twice
MobileNetV2's parameters. In the fine-tuned case, the two networks are almost at
the same level. The
gap between the frozen runs shows how well each network's learned ImageNet
features happen to
transfer to $64\times64$ satellite images.
Once fine-tuned, EfficientNet-B0 offers no meaningful accuracy gain over
MobileNetV2 for nearly twice the memory, so MobileNetV2 is the better edge
candidate of the two.

The supplementary rows show that increasing the resolution from $64\times64$ to
$224\times224$ gives both frozen backbones a gain of a few points, but the
fine-tuned models gain less than one point. A possible explanation is that a
frozen network's filters were learned at ImageNet's scale, so upsampling the
input
is the only way to bring the data to them. Instead, fine-tuning moves the
filters to the data, after which resolution becomes less important. For each of
the two
networks, the fine-tuned $64\times64$ model outperforms the frozen
$224\times224$ one. It also does about $(224/64)^2\approx12$ times fewer
operations per image, because a convolution layer's cost depends on the $H\times W$
of its output. For an edge device,
fine-tuning at native resolution is the cheaper way to get accuracy.

Even the smallest of these models is one to two orders of magnitude larger than
Model~B (Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison}). Whether the additional accuracy is
worth that memory is the
question Section~\ref{sec:task6} answers.

The training curves (Figures~\ref{fig:sota-loss}--\ref{fig:efficientnet-224-loss})
show the difference between the two approaches for both networks. Each frozen
run converges at a higher loss than its respective fine-tuned one. The frozen
EfficientNet-B0 curves are also visibly noisier than MobileNetV2's. After the
first few epochs, both its training and validation losses fluctuate without
converging, and at $224\times224$ the lowest validation loss happens to fall
early,
so its selected checkpoint comes early in the run. Meanwhile, the fine-tuned
curves of
both networks are smooth and settle within a few epochs.

The noise in the frozen EfficientNet-B0 curves comes from the feature extraction
being fixed. Whereas its validation loss oscillates from epoch to
epoch, its validation accuracy changes much less, implying that the predicted classes
barely change. What does change is the confidence given to the images that
the frozen feature layers are unable to separate. Cross-entropy heavily
penalises a confidently
wrong prediction, so small updates to the prediction layer move the
loss on these borderline images much more than they move the accuracy.
MobileNetV2's frozen features have fewer misclassified images, and its loss is lower
and more stable. The two backbones also terminate in different activation functions.
EfficientNet-B0 uses the unbounded SiLU
activation function~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}, and a small fraction of images
produce
very large pooled features.
MobileNetV2's ReLU6 activation limits each feature to
six~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2}. This bounded behaviour is discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:activation-choice}. In a diagnostic check which retrained only
the prediction
layer, normalising those features had no considerable effect on reducing the
fluctuation.
Using different learning rates of $3\times10^{-4}$ and $10^{-4}$
did not remove it either, so the learning rate is not the cause.
The practical impact is in checkpoint selection. On a noisy validation curve
the lowest-loss epoch is partly random, and it need not be the
epoch with the best accuracy. Fine-tuning removes this effect because the backbone
adapts its features to EuroSAT, which is another reason the comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:task6} uses the fine-tuned runs.

The confusion matrices of the fine-tuned $64\times64$ models
(Figures~\ref{fig:mobilenetv2-confusion} and~\ref{fig:efficientnet-confusion})
show the remaining errors falling in the same few class pairs for both networks.
Highway and River are confused in both directions, possibly because at
$64\times64$ both are
thin line features a few pixels wide. There is also a substantial number of
errors among the agricultural and vegetation classes (AnnualCrop, PermanentCrop,
Pasture and HerbaceousVegetation).
